title: 道德經 第九章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 9, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 57. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 9 of the Daodejing (運夷). The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
持而盈之，
不如其已；

morph.gloss: to hold, to keep hold of
it — the object pronoun, not the genitive
is not as good as — the fixed comparative
to be like, to be the equal of
one's — standing here as the subject of the verb after it: 'one's stopping'

sentences.l:
Holding it and filling it to the brim —
not as good as one's stopping;
sentences.i: Holding a thing and going on filling it is not as good as leaving off;
sentences.n: A 不如 B is the standard comparative: A is not the equal of B, hence 'better to B'. 其已 makes a noun out of a verb by putting a possessive in front of it — 'one's stopping' — exactly as English does with 'his leaving'. 之 is the object pronoun 'it', the second of that character's two jobs from chapter 1. What the 'it' is, the poem does not say: a cup, a bow, a fortune.

sentences.t:
揣而梲之，
不可長保。

morph.gloss: to work to a point, to taper — Wang Bi glosses the line 揣末令尖, 'taper the tip to a point'; also read chuí and taken as 捶 'to hammer'
here standing for 銳 ruì, 'to sharpen to a point'; the character's own sense is a short roof-post, and its reading in this line is unsettled
can — what follows it reads passively: 'cannot be ——ed'
long, for long — cháng, not zhǎng 'to grow'

sentences.l:
Working it to a point and sharpening it —
it cannot long be kept.
sentences.i: Work it to a point and hone it, and it will not keep for long.
sentences.n: This is the chapter's sore spot. The Wang Bi text prints 梲, a word for a short roof-post, which will not do here; the old commentators take it as standing for 銳 ruì 'to sharpen', and many editions print 銳 outright. Neither the character nor its reading is settled, and 揣 is disputed too — taper, hammer, or measure. We follow the commentators' sense and say so. 不可長保 shows 可 doing what it did in chapter 1: what follows it reads passively, 'cannot be long kept'. 長 here is cháng, 'long in time'; read zhǎng it is 'to grow', and chapter 10 will use it that way.

sentences.t:
金玉滿堂，
莫之能守；

morph.gloss: the hall — the main room of a house
no one, nothing — a negative that carries its own subject
them — object pronoun, and here standing BEFORE its verb

sentences.l:
Gold and jade filling the hall —
no one them can guard;
sentences.i: Gold and jade fill the hall, and no one can keep them;
sentences.n: 莫之能守 puts the object in front of its verb: 莫 'no one', 之 'them', 能守 'can guard'. That is a rule, not a liberty — in a negated clause a pronoun object moves ahead of its verb. Take the negation away and it drops back where English expects it: 能守之, 'can guard them'. The literal line above keeps the Chinese order so you can see the inversion happen.

sentences.t:
富貴而驕，
自遺其咎。

morph.gloss: wealth and rank — a stock pair naming one condition, not two things
oneself — the reflexive, which always stands before its verb
to leave behind, to hand on — read yí, not wèi 'to present to'
blame, the fault that comes home to one

sentences.l:
Rich and honoured, and proud with it —
he leaves himself his own blame.
sentences.i: Wealth and rank, and arrogance to go with them: the man has only himself to blame.
sentences.n: 自 is the reflexive, and like the pronoun in the line before it stands in front of its verb, never after: 自遺 'leaves it to himself'. 而 here joins two states rather than two clauses — wealth and rank on one side, arrogance on the other. 咎 is not blame from outside; it is the fault that comes home.

morph.gloss: the work done, what one has achieved
to be brought to completion, to come through
the person, oneself — the character that carried chapter 7

sentences.l:
The work accomplished, the person withdraws —
heaven's Way.
sentences.i: The work done, step back: that is the Way of heaven.
sentences.n: Four characters, two clauses, and nothing joining them: 功遂 'the work is completed', 身退 'the person withdraws'. Then a last line with no verb at all — 天之道, 'heaven's Way', simply set down beside what precedes, and English has to supply 'that is'. You met that absence in chapter 1's 非常道. Other received editions print the line longer, 功成名遂身退, 'the work completed and the name achieved, the person withdraws'. The chapter is held together by rhyme: 保, 守, 咎 and 道 all fell in one Old Chinese rhyme group. In Mandarin (bǎo, shǒu, jiù, dào) the chime is broken — which is the ordinary case, and the reason a poem this old is half-silent to a modern ear.
